newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets expect a breather after wild week.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets expect a breather after wild week.

text.p: With U.S. election-related volatility behind them, Asian markets are expected to take a breather in the week ahead.
Brokers said Tokyo's Nikkei index may be a bit on edge after Japan had its own election, and Hong Kong may pause after a wild week before facing the key 13,000 resistance level.
The Dow industrials snared its second biggest weekly point gain ever, capping a week of election fireworks. The bule chip index finished up 14 points at about 6220 on Friday.
For the week, the Dow gained 197.90 points, the most since a 206.77-point surge for the week ended August 2, 1996.
The re-election of Democrat President Bill Clinton and a Republican-controlled congress, and a stable outlook for U.S. economic policy prompted Wall Street's bouyancy.
TOKYO - Stocks are seen drifting during the week ahead after the launch of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's cabinet failed to move the market last week, analysts said.

Masaaki Higashida of Nomura Securities Co Ltd expects the Nikkei average to stay between 20,500 and 21,500. "The market will nervously keep an eye on U.S. stocks, foreign investors' stance and currencies," he said.
The 225-share Nikkei average closed at 21,201.04 on Friday, up 567.98 points from its close a week earlier.
HONG KONG - Stocks are expected to pause before making a run at the next target of 13,000 points on the Hang Seng index, analysts said.
"I still believe that we are going to have a hard time getting over 13,000," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.
The index hit an all-time high of 12,898.30 on Thursday. It rose 221.89 points, or 1.77 percent, to close at 12,751.16 on Friday. Analysts saw a 12,600-12,800-point range for next week.
BANGKOK - Thai stocks were seen gaining, with the buying of telecom and bank stocks ahead of the November 17 election expected to outweigh profit-taking, brokers said.
The SET Index ended up 15.12 points at 967.6 on Friday, 55.08 points over last Friday's close. The SET-50 rose 5.21.
"We will probably see some profit taking next week but overall I think it's positive," said Pattera Dilokrungthirapop, head of research at Crosby Securities.
BOMBAY - Indian shares likely will see a technical recovery but volume will be light with players on holiday, brokers said.
"There's nothing really to push the market," said Salil Ramesh Chandra, a dealer at Rolta Share and Stock Brokers Ltd. "It might go up on technical grounds after (the) recent fall."
The markets open briefly for an auspicious "moorat" session on Sunday evening to herald the Hindu New Year, but the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) will remain closed on Monday and Tuesday.
The top-30 BSE index index dropped 81.91 points, or 2.60 percent, to 3,066.66 in the week to Thursday.
COLOMBO - Sri Lanka stocks ended the week on an upbeat note after the release of the budget for fiscal 1997 and are seen consolidating on moderate volumes, brokers said.

"The index should open to gains and keep moving up, provided it rises only a couple of points a day," said Ajit Dias Wanigasekera of Commercial Stock Brokers. Daily gains of more than five to six points would trigger profit-taking, he said.
The all share closed up 12.13 points, or 1.98 percent, at 623.11 on Friday, compared to 610.98 points a week ago.
DHAKA - Stocks ended mostly lower ahead of a holiday last Thursday, but brokers expect them to level off or rebound when trading resumes after the weekend.
They called Wednesday's fall a correction. Some said shares prices had gained so sharply the Dhaka Stock Exchange had to reduce the price movement limit for shares.

"The regulators are in fact imposing a correction. Investors got panicked by further limiting the price movement range," said broker Mostaque Ahmed after the DSE fell 233.2 points or 6.39 percent at 3,415.54 at the close of Wednesday's trading.
JAKARTA - Brokers said the market was likely to continue upward on buying of selected first- and second-liners.
"I expect the market to make further gains in the coming week. There could be correction in some stocks, but positive economic data on Indonesia will spur fresh buying," said a foreign broker.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 602.02 points, against last week's close of 570.66 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Dealers said they expect the market to trade in a narrow band during the week ahead barring any developments.
"I would expect to still see a fairly flat market," said Tony Shue of Jupiter Securities. "I would assume there will be selective buying but in a small way."
On Friday, the Composite Index closed at 1,179.60, up 1.67 points for the day and 7.12 for the week. The Second Board index was at 643.48, up 6.09 points for the day and 8.97 for the week.
MANILA - Stocks are expected to drop slightly as the market consolidates after rising eight straight sessions, brokers said.
"There's likely to be some profit-taking as the market has been up for quite a while," said Gina Roa-Dipaling, assistant vice-president at Philippine Asia Equity Securities Inc.
The main index closed at 3,090 points on Friday, up 126 points, or 4.25 percent, from last week's 2,964 points.
SEOUL - Shares are expected to be lacklustre under the pressure of margin loans and new stock supplies, brokers said.
"There's no special news out that can change the direction of the market. I think it will continue to decline for the time being," said a Schroders Securities broker.
Margin loans are near three trillion won while customer deposits at brokerage houses lag behind at 2.5 trillion. More than 1.1 trilllion won of new issues are expected this month.
On Friday, the composite index closed at 739.11, down 28.76 points, or 3.75 percent, from last Friday's close of 767.87.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said they expected shares to rise as sentiment had improved and investors had shrugged off weak economic data, looking to next year.
"The STII is presently trading at a 43-month low," one analyst said. "We should see a continuation of bottom-fishing."
On Friday, the index ended 14.50 points up at 2,117.23 compared to 2,068.17 a week earlier. The share market is closed on November 11 for a religious holiday.

SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen firmer in the near term although concerns remain over how the bourse will react if Wall Street dips from its record highs. The All Ordinaries index, closed at 2,362.1, gaining 22.7 points over the week.
"I think we can go on, but we have had a couple of pretty solid rises on Wall Street so it's a matter of whether that can be sustained," said Robert Cameron of Cameron Securities.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to consolidate at the current level on a lack of incentivies, brokers said.

After rising nearly 300 points from October 30 to the year's closing high of 6,653.65 on November 6, the index has hit strong technical resistance and may see some profit-taking, said Lin Long-hsien, analyst for United Securities.
"This period of quiet trading will not cause a plunge, but it should last the entire next week," he said.
On Friday, the index ended at 6,581.96, up from 6,455.11 last Friday. The index is seen moving between 6,520 and 6,610 points next week.
WELLINGTON - Brokers are awaiting a board meeting of market leader Telecom on Thursday for possible share buy-back news.

"Maybe you might see another kick-up in Telecom's share price if it does go ahead and you might see the rest of the market follow suit. At the moment, we're all waiting for Thursday," said Luke Koekoek, broker at J.B. Were and Son.
The NZSE-40 capital index eased four points to end the week at 2,334.89, a rise of 12 points from last week.
